title: The decision tree
sub: Subsets and Permutations: choose and undo, saying 2ⁿ·n and n!·n out loud, subsets as bitmasks
cards/0/title: The problem and the “list them all” signal
cards/0/body:
Subsets (LeetCode #78). Given an array of distinct numbers nums, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10, return all of its subsets, including the empty one, in any order. For [1, 2, 3] there are eight: [], [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3].

The signal for exhaustive search is that the problem asks you to list all the options: all subsets, all permutations, all placements, all partitions. The answer itself is exponential: there are 2ⁿ subsets, and each has to be written out. So nothing can beat O(n·2ⁿ), and the “naive solution” here is the solution — the only question is how to walk the options without duplicates and without wasted work.

It is a different story when the question is how many options, the minimum, or is it possible. Then you don’t have to write out every option, and there is often a polynomial solution — dynamic programming, the second half of this unit. Brute force there is the baseline, not the answer.

Small limits are a signal too: n ≤ 10–20 almost always means “you can enumerate”.
cards/1/q: Where is enumerating every option the actual solution, not a naive baseline? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: Print every way to arrange 8 items in 8 slots
cards/1/options/1: Print every set of 12 perks whose total cost fits the budget
cards/1/options/2: How many subsets of an array of 10⁴ numbers sum to k ≤ 1000
cards/1/options/3: The minimum number of coins that make the sum 10⁴
cards/1/options/4: Print every word of length 5 over the letters A–D
cards/1/explain: Arrangements, perk sets and words ask you to list every option: the answer itself is exponential (8!, up to 2¹², 4⁵), and only enumeration can write it out. “How many subsets” and “minimum coins” ask for a number, not a list: with n = 10⁴, enumerating 2ⁿ is impossible, while DP computes the answer in polynomial time — that is lessons 3–4.
cards/2/title: Take it or leave it: choose, recurse, undo
cards/2/body:
A subset is n decisions in a row: for each number, “take” or “skip”. Draw these decisions as a tree: at level i we decide the fate of nums[i], every node has two children, at depth n there are 2ⁿ leaves, and each leaf is one subset.

We walk the tree depth-first, keeping one shared list path — what was chosen on the way from the root. The step is always the same: make a choice → recurse → undo the choice. Undoing (backtracking) returns path to the state the next branch expects.

Invariant: on entry to Dfs(i), path holds exactly the chosen elements of nums[0..i−1], and it is the same after Dfs(i) returns. At a leaf (i == n) we add a copy to the answer: path itself will keep changing.

The recursion depth is n, so the call stack is no danger here (its limit was covered in the C# and Unity lesson of the first unit).
cards/2/flow/0: Dfs(i): i == n? → copy of path to the answer
cards/3/explain: A leaf is when all n numbers have been decided, i == nums.Length (with nums.Length − 1 the last number would never get its choice). The answer gets a copy: path keeps changing. The undo removes exactly the last added element; Clear would also wipe the ancestors’ choices. The “without nums[i]” branch also moves on to the next number: Dfs(i + 1), while Dfs(i) would loop forever.
cards/4/task: Walk the decision tree for [1, 2, 3]: the left branch is “take”, the right one is “skip”, the leaves are answers. The rig will stop twice and ask where the code goes next: answer from path and the order “take first, then undo and skip”.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Undo 3 and take the branch without it: [1, 2] — a leaf
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Stop: all numbers have been used
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The leaf [1, 2, 3] is saved. What does the code do next?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: The call Dfs(3) returned to Dfs(2) — the decision about the number 3. Its first branch (“take”) is done, so the code runs path.RemoveAt and the second branch Dfs(3) without the 3: another leaf, [1, 2]. The code gets back to the 2 only when Dfs(2) has returned completely.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Undo 1: path = [], next comes everything without the 1
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: All four leaves with the 1 — [1, 2, 3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [1] — are saved. What next?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: The “take 1” subtree has been walked completely, and Dfs(1) returned to the root. The root undoes its choice — path is empty again — and starts the right half of the tree: the subsets without the 1. There are no duplicates: every leaf is its own set of yes/no decisions.
cards/5/title: The cost: 2ⁿ·n and how to say it
cards/5/body:
There are 2ⁿ leaves, and each copies path — up to n elements. There are fewer internal nodes than leaves, and they do O(1) work. In total O(n·2ⁿ) time. Memory: the stack and path are O(n), the answer is O(n·2ⁿ), but that is the output size, usually named separately.

How to estimate whether it fits (the rule of thumb is about 10⁸ simple operations per second):

2ⁿ: 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³, 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹. So n ≤ 20 is comfortable, n ≈ 25 is borderline, n = 30 is out.
n!: 8! = 40 320, 10! ≈ 3.6·10⁶, 11! ≈ 4·10⁷, 12! ≈ 4.8·10⁸. Permutations can be enumerated up to n ≈ 10–11.

Out loud it sounds like this: “there are 2ⁿ leaves, at each I copy up to n elements — O(n·2ⁿ); with n ≤ 10 that is about ten thousand operations, and it can’t be faster: that many elements are in the answer itself.”
cards/6/body:
The same tree can be walked without recursion. Write a subset as a number mask: bit i is 1 if nums[i] is taken. For [a, b, c], mask 5 = 101 in binary: bits 0 and 2 are set — that is {a, c}.

Two operations make it work. 1 << n is a one shifted left by n places, that is 2ⁿ: masks from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 visit every subset exactly once. (mask >> i) & 1 shifts the mask right by i and keeps the lowest bit with a bitwise AND: that is bit i.

The complexity is the same, O(n·2ⁿ), but there is no recursion and no shared path, and a subset can be stored as a single int — handy when sets need to be compared, used as dictionary keys or counted without allocations. The limit is the bit width: the loop mask < (1 << n) on int works up to n = 30 (1 << 31 is already negative), on long with 1L << n up to 62. But enumerating 2ⁿ stops fitting in time long before that. Bits in depth are in the bitwise operations unit.

In a game: picking, out of n ≤ 20 items, the most valuable set that fits a backpack by weight is 2²⁰·20 ≈ 2·10⁷ operations. On level load or in an editor tool that is fine; every frame in Update it is not.
cards/7/q: nums = [4, 7, 9, 2]. Which subset does mask = 6 stand for?
cards/7/explain: 6 = 0110 in binary: bits 1 and 2 are set (the lowest bit is bit zero, on the right). Bit i stands for nums[i], so we take nums[1] = 7 and nums[2] = 9.
cards/7/wrong/1: [4, 7] is bits 0 and 1, mask 0011 = 3. The lowest bit of 6 is zero.
cards/7/wrong/2: [9, 2] is bits 2 and 3, mask 1100 = 12. Looks like reading the mask left to right.
cards/8/body:
Permutations (LeetCode #46). Given an array of distinct numbers, 1 ≤ n ≤ 6, return all permutations. For [1, 2, 3] there are 3! = 6.

Now each level decides not “yes/no” but which number goes into the next position: any one not used yet. The first level has n options, the second n − 1, … — n! leaves. To avoid scanning path for “was it used”, keep a flag array used: an O(1) check.

The template is the same: place (used[i] = true, path.Add) → recurse → take back both changes. Forgetting to reset used[i] means losing that number for all later branches.

The cost: n! leaves, each with an n-element copy, and a loop over n at every node — O(n·n!). For n = 6 that is about 4 thousand operations, for n = 10 already 3.6·10⁷.
cards/9/task: Walk the permutation tree of [1, 2, 3]: each level takes any number not used yet, left to right. The rig will ask where the code goes after the first complete permutation.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: path = [1, 3]: 3 and 2 were taken back, 3 goes into the second position
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: path = [1, 2, 3] again, but from another level
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: path = [2]: everything was taken back, start with the 2
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: [1, 2, 3] is saved. What will path be on the next step?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: The third level took back the 3; there are no other free numbers there, so the call ends. The second level takes back the 2 (used[1] = false) and continues its loop: the next free index is 2, the number 3. We get [1, 3], and then [1, 3, 2]. The 2 gets the first position only when the first level’s loop moves on.
cards/10/q: This Subsets returns eight empty lists on [1, 2, 3]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/10/explain: List<int> is a reference type: res.Add(path) puts eight references to one and the same list into the answer. By the end of the walk every undo has run and path is empty — so all eight “subsets” are empty. A leaf needs a copy: res.Add(new List<int>(path)) or path.ToList().
cards/11/title: Variations: duplicates, k elements, a loop instead of yes/no
cards/11/body:
The second way to build subsets: every tree node is an answer right away, and a loop picks the next element to the right of the last one taken: Dfs(start) adds a copy of path and tries i from start. The start index guarantees that elements go in increasing index order — so {1, 2} and {2, 1} never both appear. This template is the basis of every “combinations” problem.

Exactly k elements (Combinations, #77): the same loop, but a copy goes to the answer only when path.Count == k. There are C(n, k) leaves.

Duplicates in the input (Subsets II, #90; Permutations II, #47). Sort so that equal values sit next to each other. In subsets, skip a value equal to the previous one on the same level: i > start && nums[i] == nums[i − 1]. In permutations, skip nums[i] if it equals the previous one and the previous one is not used right now: that way equal numbers are always placed in the same order.

A product of choices (Letter Combinations of a Phone Number, #17): each position has its own set of letters, up to 4ⁿ leaves.

In a game: every combination of items to check crafting recipes, every order of applying 5 buffs (5! = 120), every layout of a small set of slots. While there are 10⁵–10⁶ options, enumeration in an editor tool or on load is an honest solution.
cards/11/deep:
The lower bound. The Subsets answer holds exactly n·2ⁿ⁻¹ numbers, Permutations — n·n!. No algorithm writes out an answer faster than its size, so O(n·2ⁿ) and O(n·n!) are optimal. The subset tree has 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 nodes; the permutation tree has the sum of n!/(n − k)! over k, about e·n!: there are e − 1 ≈ 1.7 times more internal nodes than leaves, but the order is the same.

Allocations. Every leaf is a new List<int>: 2ⁿ objects. If you don’t need to return the answer, only to check every option (the best set, whether a valid one exists), don’t materialize it: check at the leaf using path or the mask — zero allocations. A local function that captures the method’s variables doesn’t touch the heap by itself: the compiler puts the captured state into a struct and passes it by reference — as long as the function is not turned into a delegate and no lambda captures the same variables.

Gray code. The masks g = i ^ (i >> 1) for i = 0, 1, 2, … differ from their neighbour in exactly one bit. So the sum or weight of the set can be updated by one element per step: O(2ⁿ) instead of O(n·2ⁿ) — noticeable when checking a set is expensive.

Permutations without used. The swap version: at level k, swap nums[k] with each nums[i], i ≥ k, recurse and swap back. The only memory is the stack. The next permutation in lexicographic order can also be produced without recursion (Next Permutation, #31): find the first descent from the right a[i] < a[i + 1], swap a[i] with the rightmost element greater than it, reverse the tail after i. The .NET base library has no such function.

Unity. The recursion depth equals n — for exhaustive search it is never the problem: the exponent runs out before the stack does. The problem is time: 2·10⁷ operations take tens, even hundreds of milliseconds, that is anywhere from a few frames to a dozen. Heavy enumeration goes into an editor tool, onto loading, or into a Job: masks are plain ints, easy to hand out to threads in ranges in an IJobParallelFor.
cards/12/q: You are solving Subsets out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: are the numbers distinct? is the empty set needed? does order matter? what is n?
cards/12/items/1: Point out that the answer itself holds 2ⁿ sets — so enumeration is the solution
cards/12/items/2: Idea: a “take / skip” decision tree, one shared path and backtracking
cards/12/items/3: Write the code, saying: at a leaf — a copy of path, after the recursion — RemoveAt
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(n·2ⁿ) time, O(n) for the stack and path plus the answer itself
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: n = 1, duplicates in the input — sort and skip equal values
cards/12/explain: Clarifying duplicates and the empty set changes the code, so it comes first. The argument “the answer itself is exponential” settles the question of a fast solution before the interviewer asks it. A run on two numbers checks both the undo and the copy.
